newsitem.title: SPAIN: Possible EMU delay seen risky for Spain.
newsitem.headline: Possible EMU delay seen risky for Spain.

text.p: A delay in European monetary union would buy Spain time to solidify its new-found economic stability, but analysts said on Friday the downside risks far outweigh any benefits.
Talk of possible delay resurfaced this week when Germany's powerful central bank and government clashed over Bonn's plan to revalue gold assets in a move to meet EMU convergence criteria.
The prospect of a less fiscally prudent government in France after Sunday's run-off parliamentary election added to the uncertainty.
"If Spain does make the criteria, obviously they want EMU to start on time," said Heather Richardson, European economist at UBS in London.
"Otherwise they have to keep inflation and the budget deficit down for years. They can't lapse at all or they might not be included when it does go ahead."

Spain has planned for fiscal austerity through 2000. But without the holy grail of EMU, it would be difficult to justify more of sacrifices the Spanish public has already been called on to make for the sake of an overriding desire to be a full partner in Europe after decades of isolation.
A diplomat based in Madrid pointed out that putting off EMU's launch would carry political as well as economic risks.
"If there is not going to be a euro, why suffer the political pain of cutting spending here, reducing there. It makes it harder to hold the line on spending."

The Spanish government appears confident it will qualify for the first stage of European economic and monetary union (EMU), set to start on January 1, 1999. That view has been embraced by the European Commission and increasingly by financial markets.

With inflation below 2.0 percent, interest rates at historic lows, the peseta stable, growth steady and deficits and debt on the decline, Spain is enjoying a level of economic stability unseen in its modern history.

It already meets three of the five Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria to qualify for the euro launch and asset markets have performed strongly over the past year with foreign direct investment also rising.

Still, unemployment remains a problem at the highest rate in the European Union. And Spain has not yet reached the Maastricht goal to reduce budget deficits to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, although the government expects to do so by the end of the year.

"It would make things easier for Spain if they had another year," said Richardson. "Unemployment is a big problem and by that time, the labour reform would kick in...it would be able to bring down the debt and deficit."
Others said the risks inherent in a delay were too great.
"The word delay would be very negative," said Marco Pianelli, senior economist at Nomura in London. "It would raise serious questions over the credibility of the convergence path."
The loss of credibility could trigger a "potentially explosive" phase of heavy currency fluctuations that would punish Spain and other European countries, Pianelli said.
"The markets would see it (a delay) as a way to shelve the project...That would be very damaging for European exchange rates."

A delay could also pose internal political problems for Spain's minority government. The ruling Popular Party now counts on the support from the Catalan nationalist coalition, Convergence and Unity (CiU), for a majority in parliament.
The Catalans have pledged support for the government at least until mid-1998, when the decision is expected to be taken on who is in or out of EMU's first wave.
The Catalans may stay on if the launch is delayed but if not, the government risks being left without a parliamentary majority in late 1998 when they need to pass the 1999 budget.
